title: Why a model should not approve its own actions
lede: The idea behind NEXUS CORE: keep intelligence, authority and execution in separate components.

figure.caption: Authority begins at the boundary. Everything to its left is untrusted proposal.

p: An agent that both proposes and authorizes its own actions collapses two separate questions into one: what should be done, and what is permitted. A language model is a probabilistic function of its context. Its output can be fluent, confident and wrong, and it can be steered by any text that reaches its context window, including files, web pages and user messages.

When authority sits inside that function, a single **adversarial input** or an ordinary mistake is enough to change what the system does. The model's confidence carries no information about whether an action is safe.

NEXUS CORE treats the model as an **untrusted, probabilistic component**. A planner produces a candidate plan, and that plan is data. Authority belongs to a governance stage implemented as ordinary code, whose decisions do not vary with the model's phrasing.

The system executes only what that stage released, through a layer that cannot be talked into doing more. The trust boundary sits between proposal and decision, which is where the trust actually changes.

A policy engine evaluates each proposed step against explicit rules and returns a decision such as allow, deny or hold for approval. **Determinism** is the point: the same plan under the same policy produces the same decision, so rules can be unit tested, reviewed in a diff and changed deliberately.
A control that depends on how a prompt happens to be worded cannot be tested in that sense. A control expressed as code can.

Sensitive operations, including financial actions, are designed to enter a **held state**. Leaving that state requires an approval event that originates outside the model, so a persuasive explanation inside a model response cannot satisfy it.
The principle behind it is simple. A response that claims an action was authorized, or that it happened, is not evidence of either. Evidence is a state transition in the system, written down.

Governance decisions and executions are written to an audit record using **audit hashes**. Chaining records makes silent modification detectable, which turns the history into something that can be verified instead of trusted.
This also changes debugging. When a run behaves unexpectedly, the question becomes which stage made which decision, and the record answers it.
A corrector stage examines execution results and intermediate state for errors. It is deliberately bounded: it may propose repairs, and every repair re-enters the same governance path.
Without that constraint, error recovery would become a second, unreviewed route to authority, which is exactly the property the architecture is trying to remove.

The separation adds components, state and latency, and each extra stage is more code to test. It does not make a model correct. It **narrows what an incorrect model can do** and makes failures attributable to a stage.
This note describes design intent. It makes no claim about test results or production readiness.

title: NEXUS CORE, end to end
lede: How a request moves through a governance-first agent prototype: what is real, what is simulated and what is still planned.

figure.caption: The model proposes a plan. A separate, deterministic layer decides whether anything runs, and every stage leaves a record.

p: NEXUS CORE treats a language model as an untrusted, probabilistic engine. The model can interpret a request, choose an approach, propose tool calls and revise a rejected plan. It cannot authorize its own proposal: every plan passes through a deterministic, **fail-closed** policy check before anything executes.

This note describes the current working prototype. It is a governance-first orchestration pipeline in active development, not a finished sandbox or a production-ready autonomous platform. Where something is simulated or only planned, the note says so.

The interface is a Next.js and React Command Center where users submit tasks, inspect conversations, watch pipeline events and review governance decisions. It reads a Server-Sent Events stream, so blocked decisions and the correction loop are visible instead of hidden behind a single answer.

A FastAPI backend exposes authentication, projects, conversations, messages, task streaming, artifacts and audit records. It validates request bodies, resolves who is calling and hands orchestration to one orchestrator. A demo identity exists for development. It is not an acceptable default for a multi-user deployment.

Before planning, the orchestrator passes up to the last 20 messages to a semantic understanding step that infers intent, task type, complexity, ambiguity and security signals, with a fallback if the model is unavailable. A separate pattern classifier checks the original input for instruction overrides, prompt extraction, fake system messages and obfuscation. These signals inform the plan and add defense in depth. They are evidence, not authorization.

A router maps the task to a category, model configuration and reasoning mode, using semantic hints with a keyword fallback. The planner agent, ELLA, then turns the request into a structured execution plan: a summary, a response mode and ordered steps, each with an action, a target, parameters and a rationale.

Governance evaluates that plan. If it is blocked, a correction agent, JANE, may revise it. Approved plans reach the execution layer, which dispatches supported actions and collects logs and artifacts. SQLite stores projects, conversations, messages, tasks, artifacts and the audit records.

A request starts in the frontend and opens a streaming endpoint. The orchestrator creates a task record, loads earlier messages and stores the new user message. Semantic understanding and the security classifier run, the router picks a category, and the planner proposes a structured plan that is parsed and validated against a shared schema.

Governance then evaluates the plan independently of the planner. A blocked plan may go to the correction agent, and the revised plan must pass governance again. Repeated rejection ends the task. An approved plan is executed, results and artifacts are collected, and the response and task state are saved. Each stage is streamed to the client as it completes and written to the audit record.
One honest edge: when a client disconnects, the pipeline stops advancing, but a model request that is already in flight cannot be guaranteed to stop immediately.

sections.h: A plan that parses is not a plan that is safe
p: Model output goes through defensive JSON extraction and schema validation before it becomes a plan. That establishes structure only. A well-formed plan can still ask for something dangerous, which is why validation and authorization are separate steps.

The planner also has three response modes: answer directly, ask for clarification without inventing steps, or execute tools. The distinction keeps a vague request from being turned into confident-looking actions.

The governance layer is plain Python rules, not another model asked whether the plan seems safe. It inspects the flattened content of each step for dangerous system commands, destructive SQL, sensitive file paths, path traversal and secret exfiltration, and it rejects blocked action names. The result is a structured verdict: the decision, the rules that fired, the security signals and a reason.
If evaluation itself throws an exception, the verdict is **blocked**, never implicit approval. The same input and configuration give the same decision, and a rejection always names its reason.
The limit matters just as much: a pattern-based evaluator is only as complete as its patterns. It is not a full policy language and not proof of safety.

When a plan is blocked, the correction agent receives the rejected plan and the governance feedback and tries again. Its output is more model-generated data, so it is parsed, validated and evaluated exactly like the original. Without that rule, the correction path would be a bypass around the policy boundary.

The loop is bounded, with a default maximum of two correction attempts, so a stubborn plan ends in rejection instead of retrying forever. It does not provide human approval, rollback or protection against partial effects from future real integrations.

sections.h: What is simulated, and why it matters
p: Most actions in the prototype are simulated. Read-only web search is the one documented real external tool. Importing a tool module does not mean its action has a production-safe execution path.

The distinction matters because a simulated file write shows orchestration behavior. It does not prove filesystem isolation, and a governance verdict is not a replacement for a separate permission check at the real tool boundary. The code also sanitizes search results and classifies known injection patterns. Those are supporting defenses, not proof that hostile content is neutralized.

sections.h: An audit trail with honest limits
p: Each stage writes an append-oriented audit record: the task, stage, label, details, a timestamp, the previous record's hash and its own SHA-256 hash. The event stream carries the record hash, so the interface can show a hash-linked timeline and whether the chain verifies. Deleting a conversation or a message does not touch the audit tables, so the execution history can outlive the content.

Hash linking detects some kinds of tampering. It does not make the database immutable, because someone who can rewrite the records can recompute the chain. Stronger integrity would need independent checkpoints or signatures.

sections.h: A bug worth telling: timestamps that sort wrong
p: Timestamps were stored as text, and Python's default ISO format drops the fractional seconds when the microseconds are exactly zero. Mixed representations then sort and compare unexpectedly as strings. That affects message order and any operation that deletes a message and everything after it.

The fix is to always serialize with explicit microsecond precision, so every stored timestamp has the same shape and text order matches time order. No separate regression test for this is claimed yet.

Built in the prototype: the API and Command Center, structured plans with shared schemas, semantic understanding and prompt classification, routing, the planner and correction agents, fail-closed governance, bounded correction with re-evaluation, SSE pipeline events, SQLite persistence, hash-linked audit records with chain verification, multi-turn context, full-text message search where the SQLite runtime supports it, and mostly simulated execution with one real read-only search path.

Still planned or incomplete: enforced production authentication with verified isolation between users, authorization enforced at each real tool boundary, a general human-approval workflow, real integrations with scoped permissions, complete automated security and regression tests, independent audit checkpoints, rate limiting and monitoring, and embedding-based memory in place of today's full-text search.

The first priority is making authorization an execution invariant: a typed contract between governance and execution, so every real tool call traces back to the exact approved action, target and parameters, and anything unknown or malformed is rejected by default.

After that come reproducible security tests that record false positives and false negatives, lifecycle failure tests for timeouts, disconnects and corrupted audit chains, one narrowly scoped real integration with every allowed, blocked, denied and failed path tested, signed audit checkpoints, and reliability baselines before any scaling decisions. The longer plan is in the next note.

title: Where NEXUS CORE goes next
lede: A planned roadmap for durable missions, governed multi-agent work and approvals, with the safety primitives built first.

figure.caption: Safety and reliability primitives come first. Autonomy expands only inside enforceable authority.

p: Everything in this note is a planned extension. None of it is a claim about the current implementation, which is a request-and-response orchestration prototype. The architecture note says what exists today.

The principle does not change: models are **untrusted probabilistic engines**. Autonomy decides how independently a mission progresses. It never gives a model control over the rules that authorize its actions.

The order is deliberate. First come execution-boundary authorization and typed capability contracts. Then a durable mission runtime with checkpoints, cancellation and recovery. Then governed multi-agent coordination with independent verification, followed by approval workflows and explicit autonomy levels, then persistent memory and mission-wide tracing, and only then broader tool integrations.
The order may change as testing exposes dependencies. What should not change is the rule behind it: expand the ability to act only after the controls around acting are enforced and tested.

Today a task is one request and one plan. The plan is to move to missions with an explicit lifecycle: objectives, constraints, deadlines, completion criteria and cancellation. Work would be split into dependency-aware graphs, run by persistent workers with checkpoints, retries and timeouts.

A mission could pause for missing information, a policy decision or human approval, then resume from recorded state. Scheduled and event-triggered runs would carry bounded retries and resource budgets.

Specialized agents would handle planning, research, coding, testing, analysis, security review, execution and verification, coordinated by an agent that delegates work, tracks dependencies and decides when a mission is done. Contracts between agents would be typed, and one agent's output is treated as untrusted input to the next, even inside the same system.
Agents cannot grant themselves permissions or change their own authority boundaries. Specialization must never create an ungoverned execution path.

sections.h: A capability layer instead of wired-in tools
p: Individually wired tools would give way to a registry and an execution gateway. Each capability declares its parameters, required permissions, side effects, risk class and limits. Authorization is enforced at the execution boundary, not only when the plan is made, with least-privilege credentials, target restrictions, quotas, timeouts and isolation per capability. Invocations are recorded with secrets redacted.
Having a tool never implies unrestricted authority to use it.

Four levels are planned. Advisory returns recommendations and executes nothing. Supervised prepares and validates plans, then asks for approval before designated actions. Bounded autonomous executes permitted actions within configured permissions, budgets and targets. Mission-based pursues a persistent objective through many governed steps and stops or asks for help when it reaches a boundary.

The exact permission model and the transitions between levels are still to be designed. Governance would judge the actual action, target, parameters and current authority, never the model's explanation of its intent.

sections.h: Approval that binds to what was reviewed
p: An approval request would carry the proposed action, the affected resources, a risk class, the rationale and the evidence, with approve, reject, cancel, pause and resume. An approval would be bound to the exact plan version that was reviewed and invalidated when something material changes.
A rejection or a policy violation can never be quietly reinterpreted as permission to continue. A governance APPROVED verdict stays distinct from a human decision.

Short-term conversation, mission state, long-term memory and retrieved reference material would be kept apart. Semantic retrieval with embeddings, and possibly graph relationships, would sit beside today's text search. Every stored item would carry provenance, ownership and access control, and the system would tell observed facts, user instructions, inferences and unverified agent output apart.
Memory can inform a decision. It must not silently expand authority or override a higher-priority control.

sections.h: Verification that does not trust the worker
p: Acceptance criteria would be defined before execution where possible, checked by independent reviewers or deterministic validators. The system would ask for evidence of completion instead of accepting a successful tool response or a confident claim. Disagreement between planner, executor and verifier goes to correction or to a person.

Verification results would be stored separately from the claims of the agent that did the work, and adversarial tests would cover prompt injection, malicious tool results, parameter manipulation and attempts to bypass governance.

JANE would grow from plan correction into security monitoring: correlating events across agents and missions, spotting repeated blocks, escalation attempts and abnormal resource use, and suspending a mission at configured thresholds. It could report and recommend, but it must not rewrite the rules that constrain it.

Audit would gain mission-wide traces, cost and latency tracking, and externally anchored or signed checkpoints, because hash links alone do not stop someone who can rewrite the database. The interface would grow from a conversation view into mission control: execution graphs, live traces, approval queues, permissions and budgets, showing what the system is doing and why.

Beyond that are controlled software-development and deployment workflows, browser and application automation, and, where proper safety systems exist, device control. Each needs its own threat model, tests and safeguards. None is implied by today's simulated tools.
The long-term goal is a persistent, multi-agent automation system that can plan, act, observe, verify, recover and keep working toward objectives inside explicit, enforceable authority boundaries.

title: Sending a message to the right place
lede: Intent routing in a WhatsApp assistant, and why a message that looks like a command is not one.

figure.caption: Routing is a decision made from intent and conversation state, not a lookup on keywords.

p: Messaging traffic is short, fragmentary and context-dependent. People mix languages, abbreviate, and answer a question asked ten messages ago. Treating each message as an isolated string to match against keywords produces a system that is brittle in exactly the situations users find most natural.
ELLA is designed to select a handler from two inputs: the **intent** of the message and the **state of the conversation**. Lexical overlap with a command is weak evidence on its own.

The cost of an error is asymmetric. A false positive runs a specialized behavior the user never asked for, while a missed match usually costs one more message. Routing is tuned with that asymmetry in mind.
When a reference cannot be resolved there are two failure modes: ask, or guess. Asking costs one round trip. Guessing risks a wrong action and a loss of trust.
The design prefers the **clarifying question** whenever the ambiguity changes which handler should run, and a plain reply when it does not.
Groups add addressing and threading problems. The assistant must decide whether it is being spoken to, which earlier message a reply refers to, and how much of the shared context is relevant.
These are routing inputs, not formatting details. Getting them wrong produces replies that are technically valid and socially wrong.
A chat assistant sits in front of third-party services that fail: model providers, media sources, storage. The contract is that an operation is reported as complete only when it **completed**.
A plain error is preferable to a confident message describing something that did not happen. The first is recoverable by the user, and the second is a silent data-integrity problem.

Awareness of Nigerian English and Pidgin matters for routing as much as for tone, because the same sentence can mean different things depending on how it is written. A router that misreads the message cannot choose the right handler, however good the handlers are.

Voice and call work is maintained separately from production behavior and is not presented as available until it is verified. Developer and administrative controls are likewise separated from the user-facing surface.
This note describes design priorities. It makes no claim about test results.

title: Designing a status check that does not cry wolf
lede: How the live Live, Down and Status unavailable chips on this site decide what to say.

figure.caption: Two independent requests feed a three-valued verdict. Inconclusive evidence is never reported as down.

p: Next to each deployed project the site shows **Live**, **Down** or **Status unavailable**. The check measures one thing: whether the deployed site answers an HTTP request. It does not measure whether the backend behind that site works, and the labels are worded to say so.

sections.h: Why the check runs on the server
p: A browser may not read the status of another origin unless that origin sends the right cross-origin headers. Each project therefore has a small serverless function on this site that makes the request and returns a short JSON verdict.
The browser only talks to its own origin, which removes the cross-origin problem and keeps the logic in one place.
Each function requests exactly one hard-coded address. Nothing in the incoming request, such as a query parameter, can change the target.
That removes the class of **server-side request forgery** problems an open endpoint that fetches any URL would create. The functions also accept only GET and HEAD and answer anything else with 405.

Every check issues two requests with a nine second timeout. A response below 500 counts as live, including redirects and 404 pages, because the host answered. Two server errors count as down. Everything else is reported as unknown, including timeouts, network errors and mixed results.
The verdict function is a pure mapping from two observations to one of three values, which is what makes it easy to test.

Free hosting tiers sleep when idle. The first request after a quiet period can time out while the service wakes. Reporting that as down would be a **false alarm**, so inconclusive evidence is shown as Status unavailable.
A monitor that raises alarms it cannot justify trains people to ignore it.

Responses are sent with no-store, so each answer reflects the moment of the check. The page asks again every minute while the tab is visible and stops while it is hidden, which keeps load proportional to attention.

The decision logic has unit tests that mock the network and cover live, down, timeout, mixed and rejected-method cases for each endpoint. A browser test serves the site, stubs the endpoints and asserts that every chip reads Live, Down and Status unavailable correctly, including when the endpoint itself fails.

title: How this portfolio is built
lede: A static site with a readable build step, content as data and guardrails that run on every change.

figure.caption: Pages are generated from data, committed as plain files and served as static assets.

p: The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A single Python script that uses only the standard library generates every page from JSON content files. There is no framework runtime to hydrate and no bundler to configure, so what is deployed is what is committed.

Projects, technologies, design notes and the landing page live under content/. The generator renders them into pages, a sitemap and a robots file, and project pages share one template. Adding a project means editing **data**, not markup.

The build fails if an em or en dash appears in any generated page. A browser test visits every page at four viewport widths and checks for console errors, horizontal overflow, undersized tap targets and broken internal links.
Constraints that are checked by machines stay true after the tenth edit.

The content is in the HTML. Animation, the project rail, the typed code and the pinned scroll story are layered on by script and by newer CSS features, and each falls back to a plain layout when it is unavailable, including with JavaScript off.

Animation uses transform and opacity, runs only while an element is visible, and respects the **reduced-motion** preference. Scroll-linked effects share one throttled listener and an IntersectionObserver, so the cost does not grow with the number of animated elements.

sections.h: Contact details stay out of the markup
p: Email, WhatsApp and social links are assembled in the browser, so the HTML source carries no readable contact details. This reduces casual scraping and does not claim to be a security boundary.
A push to a branch produces a Vercel preview. Merging to main publishes. The status functions deploy alongside the pages and are covered by their own unit tests.
